evidence.fact: Commercial AI skin-analysis tools already scan a face from a photo, detect about 15 skin concerns such as redness, wrinkles and texture, and then generate a personalised product routine with explanations.

Consumer AI skincare apps recommend products based on skin type and explain which ingredient targets which concern, although they state their advice is informational only. The salon version of this task still depends on in-person skin assessment, demonstrating how to apply products and building client trust during the service.

State cosmetology boards regulate skin-care services, meaning the physical treatments, under the license. Makeup demonstrations and product advice are not described as acts only a licensee may perform, so no human sign-off is required to recommend products.
One vendor's AI agent connects to Booqable rental software. It reads live inventory to check availability and can create bookings and look up customers. Staff still handle the physical logistics.
Rently's AI agent on WhatsApp answers questions about availability, pricing and requirements, and records reservations in the rental system. Complex requests and VIP customers go to human staff.
Bookyt's rental chatbot matches a customer's question to the rental offering, asks for any missing details, and points to booking. This covers much of the discussion about type, quality and quantity.
Conversational-commerce AI agents already greet online shoppers proactively, answer questions and recommend products to identify needs. Fin puts the 2026 market at about $10–14B.
Gorgias says proactive AI engagement drove 50% of conversation-driven purchases during BFCM 2025, which shows AI handling the greet-and-qualify step in digital channels. This is vendor data.

Agentic commerce tools such as Salesforce Agentforce Commerce work in digital storefronts. On the shop floor, greeting and reading customers face to face needs physical presence, which a bodiless agent lacks, so its role there is limited to helping staff (product lookup, suggestions).

Microsoft Brand Agents bring the advice a store associate would give into a chat on the retailer's website, including guidance, upselling and cross-selling. Google, OpenAI, Shopify and PayPal are building similar conversational shopping where customers compare and buy in one place.

In stores, AI copilots and voice-headset assistants support human associates by giving them product, inventory and recommendation data in real time. The associate still serves the customer face to face and physically finds the items.

Manhattan Active Omni's Store Associate Agent answers natural-language questions about inventory and customer behavior, so an agent can handle the 'locate or obtain' step through software. Gaps in universal carts, APIs and product data still limit full deployment.

AI travel chatbots and agents already put together information tailored to the traveler's itinerary and nationality. This includes visa and entry rules, transit requirements, local customs and etiquette, so the main step of assembling the information is automated.

No-code AI agents automatically check visa and entry eligibility by nationality and destination and alert users when requirements change. Guidance for travel agents still advises checking AI drafts against official sources.

IATA Timatic gives travel agents passport, visa and health requirements for over 220 countries, online or by API. That makes the authoritative regulation data digitally reachable, so an agent can send it to the customer by email or in a document instead of handing over a printed brochure.

Vendor pages describe AI agents that run program enrollment from start to finish. They ask qualifying questions, send eligible applicants on to enrollment, offer waitlists or other programs to the rest, and follow up automatically by email or SMS. These are marketing claims and have not been independently checked.

The same vendor offers agents for government health-program enrollment. They pre-screen applicants on household income, family size and participation in other programs, and they collect registration details.

A guide on automating financial aid recommends that AI handle screening, flagging, document requests and status outreach, while humans make the final eligibility or award decisions. Low-confidence cases should go to a human, and every automated decision should be logged.

AI tools such as S7 PLC Buddy, which uses Claude, can read live PLC diagnostics over the network and suggest likely causes. The vendor notes that the operational data agents need is spread across separate systems like SCADA, historians and fleet software.
Agent products for field technicians combine live readings, error logs and maintenance history to help with troubleshooting, but a technician still does the hands-on work.

Under NFPA 70E, touching energized parts with probes or test equipment counts as energized work. It must be done by a qualified person physically present with the right PPE, so diagnosing with meters and scopes needs someone on site.

Vendor pages say hotel revenue-management systems (RoomPriceGenie, PricingService.ai, RoomRaccoon/Pricepoint) set room rates on their own from competitor prices, booking pace and occupancy, push them to the PMS and channel manager, and offer an autopilot mode. These are vendor claims, not independent results.

Hotel budgeting tools such as Otelier TruePlan pull actuals from PMS, POS and accounting systems and use pre-built drivers to cut budget build time. Building the budget still needs input from department heads, and the owner or GM must approve how funds are split between departments.
Vendor buyer's guides say AI budgeting and forecasting software automates driver-based forecasts and budget updates. I found no evidence of fully autonomous budget approval or fund allocation.
